topic: Real-time & background: WebSockets, push & scheduled work

questions.question: Your chat app gets messages via push. What is the recommended way to use FCM / APNs here?
options: Rely on push for everything and drop the server sync API, because push already reaches every installed device
Send one push per message with every attachment base64-encoded so the app never needs to make a network call
Treat a push as a hint that something changed, then fetch the actual messages from your server and dedupe them
Put the full message history in each push payload, since push delivery is guaranteed and preserves order
questions.explanation: Both FCM and APNs cap payloads at about 4 KB, can collapse or drop messages, and do not promise order. So the robust pattern is push as a wake-up or display signal, with the server as the source of truth that the app syncs from. Designs that assume guaranteed, ordered push lose messages in exactly the cases users notice.

questions.question: Neither FCM nor APNs guarantees that every message is delivered or that messages arrive in order, so the client needs a way to recover missed events from your server.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Messages can be throttled, collapsed, expire while the device is offline, or be dropped (for example after a force-quit on iOS or when a user disables notifications). Ordering is not promised either. Clients therefore keep a last-seen marker and sync the gap from the server.

questions.question: You need to upload diagnostics 'sometime soon, on Wi-Fi and while charging', and it must survive app restarts. Which tools fit on each platform?
options: Android: WorkManager with unmetered-network and charging constraints. iOS: a BGProcessingTask via BGTaskScheduler requiring power and network
Android: a foreground service started at launch. iOS: a background URLSession started from applicationDidEnterBackground
Android: an exact AlarmManager alarm every hour. iOS: a silent push from the server every hour to trigger the upload
Android: a coroutine in viewModelScope that waits for Wi-Fi. iOS: a Task on the main actor that waits for charging
questions.explanation: Deferrable, constraint-based, persistent work is what WorkManager and BGTaskScheduler (BGProcessingTaskRequest has `requiresExternalPower` and `requiresNetworkConnectivity`) are built for. Foreground services are for user-visible ongoing work, and exact alarms or silent pushes are heavy-handed and throttled. ViewModel or in-process tasks die with the process.

questions.question: Your WebSocket server restarts and a million clients disconnect at the same moment. Why add random jitter to the exponential reconnect backoff?
options: So the first reconnect attempt happens sooner on average, which gets the user back online with less waiting
So clients spread out their retries instead of reconnecting in synchronised waves that overload the restarted server
So messages sent during the outage are replayed in order once the connection is established again
So TLS session resumption works, since resumed sessions must not all start in the same second
questions.explanation: Without jitter every client computes the same 1s, 2s, 4s... schedule and they hit the server together: a thundering herd that can knock it over again. Randomising (e.g. 'full jitter': a random delay between 0 and the backoff cap) flattens the load. Jitter is about server load, not latency, ordering or TLS.

questions.question: After a WebSocket reconnect, how should a chat client make sure it has not missed messages sent while it was disconnected?
options: Reload the full history of every conversation on each reconnect so the local copy is never incomplete
Trust TCP, which guarantees in-order delivery, so the server resends what the old connection never delivered
Keep the old socket in a 'paused' state so the server can buffer messages there until the client resumes it
Track the last server sequence number per conversation, request everything after it on reconnect, and dedupe by message ID
questions.explanation: TCP's guarantees end when the connection does; a new socket knows nothing about the old one. A per-conversation sequence number (or opaque cursor) lets the client ask for exactly the gap, and IDs make overlaps harmless. Reloading everything is too expensive on mobile data, and a dead socket cannot be resumed.

questions.question: Your messaging pipeline gives at-least-once delivery over a flaky mobile network. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: At-most-once delivery is the one that requires retries, which is why it is the safer default for chat
TCP already provides exactly-once delivery end to end, so app-level IDs only matter for logging
The client must dedupe by a stable message ID, since the same message can arrive more than once
The sender needs acknowledgements, and resends until it gets an ack or gives up
'Effectively once' in practice means at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent handling on the receiver
questions.explanation: At-least-once means retry until acked, which produces duplicates, so receivers must be idempotent (usually by dedupe on ID). True exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is not achievable; you get the effect through idempotency. At-most-once means no retries, so messages can be lost.

questions.question: On iOS, an app can reliably keep receiving chat messages over a WebSocket while in the background, as long as it asked for extra background execution time when it entered the background.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Extra background time is short and ends with the app being suspended, which freezes its sockets. Real-time delivery to a backgrounded iOS app goes through APNs (with PushKit + CallKit reserved for VoIP calls). Android is more permissive with foreground services, but Doze and background limits mean push is still the dependable path there too.

questions.question: A delivery app must track the courier's location continuously for a 40-minute trip while the courier uses other apps. What is the right approach on each platform?
options: Android: a periodic WorkManager job running every minute. iOS: BGAppRefreshTask scheduled to run every minute
Android: a foreground service of location type with an ongoing notification. iOS: the location background mode with background location updates enabled
Android: an exact AlarmManager alarm every 5 seconds. iOS: silent pushes from the server every 5 seconds
Android: a coroutine in an application-scoped CoroutineScope. iOS: a detached Task kept alive by a strong reference
questions.explanation: Continuous, user-visible location work is exactly the foreground-service case on Android, and iOS supports it via the 'location' background mode and `allowsBackgroundLocationUpdates`. Periodic WorkManager work has a 15-minute minimum, and BGAppRefreshTask timing is decided by the system. Plain coroutines or tasks get stopped when the process is cached or suspended.

questions.question: Users report the chat 'looks connected' but stops receiving messages after a few idle minutes on mobile data. The socket never reports an error. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The read timeout is too short; set it to infinite so the client never gives up on a quiet connection
The server is sending frames too fast for the client; add a client-side rate limiter that discards extra frames
TCP keepalive is already on by default every few seconds, so the server must be closing sockets without sending a frame
A carrier NAT or proxy silently dropped the idle connection; add an app-level ping/pong with a timeout that triggers reconnect
questions.explanation: Mobile NATs drop idle mappings without telling either side, so the socket looks alive until you try to use it. A heartbeat (WebSocket ping/pong or an app message) both keeps the mapping warm and detects death, with the interval traded off against battery. OS-level TCP keepalive defaults are measured in hours, and an infinite timeout just hides the dead connection.

questions.question: Which statements about push delivery on current Android and iOS are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: FCM high-priority messages that do not lead to a user-visible notification may be deprioritised over time
Data-only FCM messages bypass Doze completely whatever priority you send them with
An iOS silent push will relaunch an app that the user has force-quit from the app switcher
iOS background (content-available) pushes are throttled by the system and may be delayed or not delivered
Collapse keys (FCM) and `apns-collapse-id` let a newer notification replace an older one still pending
questions.explanation: Firebase documents that high priority is meant for messages that result in a notification, and may deprioritise apps that abuse it. iOS treats background pushes as low-priority hints and budgets them; after a user force-quits, the system does not launch the app for them. Normal-priority FCM messages are batched during Doze, so priority matters.
